captions.text: Begin on Calls in an authorized Responder session.
The cards bring together a call number, name, location and assigned resources.
Read those details before choosing any response.
In this fictional department, enter Warehouse in Search calls.
The list narrows to TRAINING — Warehouse alarm, numbered DEMO-0001,
at Training site one in Chicago.
Check the name, number and address together; a familiar
word in a search result is not enough to identify an incident.
The search changes the displayed list.
It does not rename a call, dispatch anyone or change your personal status.

captions.text: Open that card to reach Call Details.
The same name and number remain at the top, followed by the nature of the call.
Here it describes reported smoke at an unoccupied training warehouse and
a Squad Three search demonstration.
The map provides context for the stored incident location.
It does not establish where your device is or whether a crew has arrived.
Route is available beside Notes, Images and Files, but we leave
it untouched while reviewing the information already supplied.

Note are visible together.

not to dispatch real resources.

carrying an assumption from the call list into your next action.

scenes.title: Keep review and response decisions distinct

captions.text: On Home, this example shows three Active Calls and zero Calls I’m On.
Those counts answer different questions.
The Status controls include Responding, Not Responding, On Scene and
Standing By; the Standing By choice remains outlined during this review.
We do not press a response button.
Use the same read-before-response pattern for fire and EMS, community-care
or mental-health teams, search and rescue, security patrols, wildland
contractors and industrial teams.
Find the correct incident, read its context and assignments, and identify
missing information before making an authorized operational response.
